title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure, not a model error in the ordinary sense. A synthetic video call was used to present a speaker as a sitting chief minister, and the fabricated identity carried the credibility that the subsequent requests for money depended on. The technical component sat inside a consumer messaging app, on a one-to-one call where no platform check, no verified account and no institutional channel stood between the caller's claimed identity and the person receiving it. The rest of the scheme was conventional advance-fee fraud, with a second impersonation of a law enforcement officer layered on top.

Catching it would have required verification of the caller's identity through a channel independent of the call itself, since the call was the only evidence offered for who was speaking. It would also have required a check at the point of payment, where a request for fees to release promised aid is the standard shape of this fraud. Nothing in the sequence described performed either check. What stopped the payments was the target's own refusal at a later demand, not any control in the system.

What is not established is who placed the call, whether the deepfake was produced by those who used it, and whether any of the people involved will be found responsible. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act, and a registration is not a finding.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29-year-old Bengaluru security guard, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9. The caller used an AI deepfake to look and sound like Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay. The caller promised Rs 11 lakh in financial aid and said a manager would handle the transfer. The manager claimed Rs 5 lakh was allotted and asked for fees. Giri first paid Rs 5,000 as exchange charges, then Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN. A person posing as a CBI officer named Thakur later demanded more than Rs 50,000 as a fine. Giri paid over Rs 1.04 lakh in total through a digital payment app.

When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, Giri refused and realized he had been cheated. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then approached Byappanahalli police. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act. This was the first such deepfake case reported in Bengaluru. Police advised people not to trust such calls or make payments based on them.
